value.overview: The Streak-chested Antpitta (Hylopezus perspicillatus) is a shy, ground-dwelling forest bird of the humid Neotropics. It spends much of its time walking or hopping through leaf litter beneath dense vegetation, where it searches for small invertebrates. Its rich brown plumage, pale facial markings, and strongly streaked chest provide useful identification features, but it is more often detected by its distinctive, repeated whistle than by sight.
value.classification: The Streak-chested Antpitta belongs to the antpitta family Grallariidae and the order Passeriformes. It is one of the ground-foraging antpittas of tropical Central and northern South America.
value.identification: This medium-sized antpitta has a compact, rounded body, short tail, and relatively long legs. The upperparts are mainly brown, while the underparts are pale to buff with conspicuous dark streaking across the breast and upper belly. It also shows contrasting pale markings around the face and throat. It usually keeps low in dense cover and may stand upright briefly before quickly disappearing into vegetation. Its loud, clear, repeated whistle is often the best way to locate it.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from parts of southern Central America through northern South America, generally in humid lowland and foothill forests. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable wet forest, especially in the Caribbean lowlands and adjacent foothills, where it uses dense understory, shaded forest floor, and areas with abundant leaf litter. It may occur in mature forest and well-developed secondary growth, but is most reliably associated with moist habitats offering dense ground cover and relatively undisturbed foraging conditions.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round in suitable humid forest; local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Information on its breeding biology is less complete than for many conspicuous bird species. Like other antpittas, it is believed to nest close to the ground or in low vegetation, using a bulky structure made from plant material. Breeding activity is associated with the rainy season in at least parts of its range, when food is abundant. The species is secretive around nesting areas, and detailed information on nest sites, clutch size, and parental care remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Streak-chested Antpitta feeds mainly on small animals found in leaf litter and soil, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. It forages by walking and making short hops beneath dense vegetation, often pausing to listen before probing or flicking aside leaves. It may also take other small invertebrates when available. Its feeding behavior is quiet and deliberate, which helps it remain difficult to observe.
value.behavior: This is a strongly terrestrial and secretive bird that usually stays in shaded understory rather than moving through the canopy. It often forages alone or in pairs and responds to danger by freezing, crouching, or slipping silently into cover. Its loud, far-carrying whistle contrasts with its unobtrusive appearance. Because it is more frequently heard than seen, patient observation along quiet forest trails is often needed for a visual encounter.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, and some populations may be affected by continuing forest loss. The species remains locally common in suitable habitat in parts of its range, including protected humid forests in Costa Rica.
